planting.note: Divide and set out established clumps in spring once soil has warmed, watering in well until new roots establish.

directions: This wild species from the Himalayan foothills and montane Southeast Asia forms arching, grass-like clumps intermediate in scale between dwarf mondo grass (O. japonicus) and the much larger white lily-turf (O. jaburan), spreading slowly by short rhizomes into a dense, weed-suppressing tuft rather than running. Pale lilac to white flower spikes nestle low in the foliage in summer, followed by small blue-black berries. Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to partial shade and keep evenly moist while clumps establish; once rooted it tolerates dry shade and root competition under trees reasonably well. Useful as a textured underplanting or path-edging grass where straight japonicus looks too fine and jaburan too coarse.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide congested clumps in spring and replant at the same depth; keep newly set divisions consistently moist until growth resumes.

directions: The smallest-growing of the commonly recognized Liriope species, this true dwarf forms tight tufts of fine, grassy evergreen leaves only a few inches tall, making it useful as a miniature edging or turf substitute where the larger L. muscari would overwhelm the scale of a small bed. Short spikes of pale lavender flowers are mostly hidden within the foliage in summer, so it is grown chiefly for its neat, low texture rather than bloom display. It increases by short offsets into a slowly expanding clump rather than spreading underground like L. spicata, so it stays well-behaved along path edges. Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled shade and divide only when clumps become crowded.

planting.note: Set divisions out in spring after the last frost in warm climates; in marginal zones grow in containers that can be sheltered over winter.

directions: Native to Taiwan, the Philippines, and parts of Indonesia, this warm-climate lilyturf forms clumping, grass-like tufts similar in habit to L. muscari but blooms noticeably later, sending up showy violet-blue flower spikes in autumn rather than summer. It is distinctly less cold-hardy than the common garden Liriope species, performing best where winters stay mild or where it can be containerized and moved under cover. Grow in humus-rich, well-drained soil in dappled to full shade, and avoid soggy winter conditions that can rot the fleshy roots. Its late bloom season makes it a useful way to extend lilyturf flowering into fall in warm gardens.
sources: Kew Royal Botanic Gardens — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide in early spring as new shoots emerge, or after flowering in late summer; keep divisions shaded and moist until roots take hold.

directions: A compact Japanese woodland species noticeably smaller and tidier in habit than most of the large hybrid hostas grown in gardens today, forming a dense mound of rounded, slightly rippled, glossy dark-green leaves on short petioles. Pale lavender flowers rise just above the foliage on slender scapes in mid- to late summer. It has long been used by Japanese and American hybridizers as a parent species behind several compact, white-margined garden cultivars. Grow in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in full to partial shade; the species resents hot, dry afternoon sun and performs best in cool woodland conditions.

planting.note: Divide small offsets in spring and replant promptly, since the shallow root systems of miniature hosta species dry out quickly if left exposed.

directions: A true miniature species native to Japan's Shikoku region, forming tight clumps of narrow, lance-shaped leaves only a few inches tall, far smaller in scale than most garden hosta cultivars. Short scapes carry purple flowers in mid- to late summer just above the compact foliage mound. It has served as an important wild parent behind many of the smallest 'mouse ear' type miniature hosta cultivars bred over the past several decades. Grow in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in part to full shade, where its diminutive size suits rock gardens, troughs, and the front edge of shaded borders rather than open beds.
